paragraphs.text: Rodan et al. (2021) reported 25 individuals from 22 families with heterozygous CACNA1C variants. Their phenotype was mainly neurological and variably included developmental delay, intellectual disability, autism, hypotonia, epilepsy, and ataxia. They did not have significant cardiac manifestations or other features of Timothy syndrome. The phenotype differed broadly between individuals with truncating variants and those with nontruncating variants.

paragraphs.text: Bozarth et al. (2018) described a girl (patient 1) of English/Ukrainian ancestry, born to nonconsanguineous parents, who had neonatal-onset epileptic encephalopathy. Tonic and tonic-myoclonic seizures began within hours of birth and evolved into epileptic tonic spasms at 3 months of age. The seizures did not respond to multiple antiepileptic drugs, although clobazam reduced them. She had profound axial and appendicular hypotonia. At 18 months she had made no developmental progress, could not fixate or track visually, and had severe sleep-wake disturbance. Other features were laryngomalacia, bilateral clubfeet, 3-4 finger and 2-3 toe syndactyly, camptodactyly, micrognathia, downturned corners of the mouth, frontal bossing, scant hair, inverted nipples, mild optic nerve hypoplasia, anal stenosis, and dysphagia requiring a gastrostomy tube. EEG showed distinctive diffuse excessive fast activity. Brain MRI, echocardiogram, and Holter monitoring were normal.

paragraphs.text: Bozarth et al. (2018) also described a family of Irish and German descent. The proband (patient 2), a girl, had tetralogy of Fallot, which was repaired at 2 months of age. At 4 months she developed severe biventricular failure with left ventricular noncompaction. She had mild dysmorphic features, including flat nasal bridge, low-set cupped ears, deep-set eyes, thin upper lip, and round face. She also had mild 2-3-4 toe syndactyly, mild developmental delay, and mild hypotonia. Her father (patient 3) had a congenital ventricular septal defect and aortic valve stenosis, learning disabilities, and ADHD. He developed focal-to-generalized tonic-clonic seizures at age 18 years, and his craniofacial features were similar to his daughter's. Bozarth et al. (2018) noted that only 3 individuals with seizures had been reported in CACNA1C-related disorders before their series. They concluded that their findings extended the phenotype to neonatal-onset epileptic encephalopathy and late-onset epilepsy and that the family showed variable expressivity. They suggested including CACNA1C on epilepsy gene panels.

paragraphs.text: Rodan et al. (2021) described 14 individuals with de novo nontruncating CACNA1C variants. All had developmental delay or intellectual disability. At last follow-up, 9 were nonverbal and 6 were nonambulatory. One had a formal diagnosis of autism and 6 others had autistic features. Twelve were hypotonic and 4 had ataxia. Prenatal findings included reduced fetal movement (3 of 14), bilateral clubfoot (2 of 14), and oligohydramnios (2 of 14). The course was consistent with a static neurodevelopmental disorder. Brain MRI was normal apart from an incidental arachnoid cyst in 1 individual and prominent cerebellar folia in another. Ten of the 14 had epilepsy, with onset ranging from 2 months to 8 years. Both generalized and focal epilepsies occurred, including West syndrome/infantile spasms, myoclonic seizures, and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. Seizures were fever-sensitive in 3 individuals and medically refractory in 4, and EEG findings were not consistent across the group. Twelve of the 14 had orthopedic abnormalities. Two had bilateral clubfoot with congenital finger contractures and 2 others had persistently adducted thumbs. Other orthopedic findings were kyphosis or scoliosis (2 of 14), congenital hip dysplasia (3 of 14), syndactyly (2 of 14), and joint hypermobility (3 of 14). ECGs were performed in 11 of these individuals and 9 were normal. One individual (P13, with a val1411-to-leu variant) had a prolonged QT interval with T-wave alternans on Holter monitoring, and another had a possible ventricular conduction delay. Echocardiograms showed only minor findings, and no individual had the physical features of Timothy syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Rodan et al. (2021) also described 11 individuals from 8 families with truncating CACNA1C variants. Most had essentially normal early motor development and walked independently. Recurrent infections were reported in 4 individuals. All 5 ECGs performed were normal.

paragraphs.text: Rodan et al. (2021) ascertained 25 individuals from 22 families through GeneMatcher and ClinVar and identified heterozygous CACNA1C variants by exome sequencing or an intellectual disability gene panel. Thirteen unrelated individuals had missense variants and 1 had an in-frame deletion. Eleven individuals from 8 families had predicted truncating variants. All missense variants affected highly conserved positions and were predicted to be damaging. Missense variants clustered in a linker segment of domain II (exon 13) and in domain IV (exon 35). Three truncating variants (R161X, W528X, and R1989X) were paternally inherited. In 1 of the 2 relatives carrying R161X, however, the variant had arisen de novo. All truncating variants except 1 located in the last exon (exon 45) were predicted to undergo nonsense-mediated decay.
